lead: Animation is the craft of giving motion to drawings, and multimedia authoring is the craft of joining those drawings, text, sound and buttons into a title a viewer can use. This unit covers both: the principles and the keyframe arithmetic behind movement, morphing and 2D/3D techniques, the metaphors authoring tools are built on, and the drawing and retouching tools you actually work with. After it you can plan a short animation, pick the right authoring metaphor for a title, and compute tween values, Bezier points, morph points and motion-blur lengths for exam questions.
about: Unit 5 explains how pictures are made to move and how a multimedia title is assembled. Chapter 5.1 gives the principles that make motion believable, and 5.2 turns poses into keyframes and tweens. Chapter 5.3 morphs one shape into another, 5.4 compares 2D and 3D techniques and tools, and 5.5 shows the card, icon and time-based metaphors authoring tools use. Chapters 5.6 to 5.9 are advanced: paint and image editing tools, layer-based photo retouching, vector paths and the pen tool, and timeline motion tweens with motion blur. Each chapter reuses the arithmetic of the one before, so the unit reads as a single pipeline from an idea to a finished, moving screen.

chapters.idea: Motion looks real only when it obeys a few rules — the body changes shape but keeps its volume, the pose reads clearly, and the spacing of frames controls the sense of weight and speed.
chapters.depth: Define animation as a sequence of still frames shown fast enough that the eye reads continuous motion; give frame rates 24 fps (film), 25 fps (PAL), 30 fps (NTSC) and cross-reference Unit 4 for formats. Name the twelve classic principles, then develop three in detail. Squash and stretch: a moving body deforms on impact and stretch when fast, but its area (2D) or volume (3D) stays roughly constant. Staging: silhouette, camera angle, background contrast and one clear action per shot, so the pose reads in one glance. Timing: how many frames an action takes and how the in-betweens are spaced; wide spacing reads fast and light, tight spacing reads slow and heavy. Add slow-in/slow-out, anticipation and arcs as the principles that support timing. Some syllabi call these the 'principles of cartoon animation' or 'Disney's twelve rules'.

figure.caption: Both curves cover the same 12 frames and the same distance; the curved one starts with tiny steps and ends with big steps, which reads as slow-in and fast-out.
figure.aria: A plot of distance against frame number for two 12-frame moves, one with equal steps per frame and one whose steps grow, showing slow-in timing.

chapters.example: A rubber ball 1 unit wide hits the floor and squashes to 0.6 of its original height over 2 frames, then rounds back in 2 more. Find its width at maximum squash if it keeps volume, and say where the timing should be tight and where wide.
chapters.trap: Squashing the ball by scaling both axes, which loses volume, and then answering that the ball 'gets smaller'. Also confusing timing (spacing of frames) with frame rate (frames per second).
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: digital images, sampling and visual perception.
chapters.leave: Frame rate standards and compression to Unit 4; the drawing tools used to make the frames to chapter 5.6.

chapters.idea: The animator draws only a few key poses and the software fills the rest by interpolating each property between them.
chapters.depth: Define a keyframe (a value fixed at a chosen frame) and an in-between (a frame computed by the system); tweening is the interpolation itself. Cover interpolation of any parameter — position, scale, rotation, opacity, colour — as a curve of value against frame. Linear, ease-in/ease-out and spline (Bezier) interpolation, and the graph editor that shows the curve. Rotation needs shortest-path handling: 350° to 10° is 20° forward, not 340° back. Tween length is a frame count, so the same tween lasts longer at 24 fps than at 30 fps. Name motion tween and shape tween here, but keep the timeline mechanics for chapter 5.9. Some syllabi call this 'in-betweening' or 'interpolation animation'.

figure.title: Linear tween, x from 20 px to 120 px over 10 frames
figure.caption: Only frames 0 and 10 are keyframes; the middle values are computed, adding 10 px every frame.
figure.aria: A table of frame numbers 0 to 10 and the tweened x position rising from 20 to 120 px in equal steps, with the two keyframe columns marked.

chapters.example: A keyframe at frame 0 holds x = 20 px and a keyframe at frame 10 holds x = 120 px. Give the linear tween values at frames 2, 4, 6 and 8, and the time at which x = 75 px.
chapters.trap: Tweening rotation the long way round, and treating the number of keyframes as the duration. The duration is the frame gap between keys.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 5.1 for why the keys are spaced unevenly.
chapters.leave: Timeline panels, motion tweens and motion blur to chapter 5.9; shape correspondence to chapter 5.3.

chapters.idea: Morphing is three steps at once — match the parts of the two shapes, move the matched parts gradually, and cross-dissolve the colours as they move.
chapters.depth: State the two ingredients: a geometric warp and a cross-dissolve, plus the correspondence that joins them. Cover control points or a mesh placed on both source and target; interpolation of each control point by P(t) = (1 − t)·P_A + t·P_B; forward warping (push source pixels to the new positions, which leaves holes) versus inverse warping (for each output pixel, look up where it came from). The cross-dissolve weight is (1 − t) for the source and t for the target. Mention mesh or vertex morphing for 3D as the same formula on vertices, and say the hard part is the correspondence, not the arithmetic. Some syllabi call this 'image metamorphosis' or 'shape blending'.

figure.title: Image morph pipeline
figure.caption: The warp and the dissolve must use the same t, or the moving shape and its colour drift apart.
figure.aria: A flow from source image to matched control points to warping at time t to cross-dissolve to the output frame.

chapters.example: Two shapes have matched control points A(0, 0) and B(100, 40). Find the intermediate point at t = 0.3 and give the source and target weights for the cross-dissolve at that instant.
chapters.trap: Calling a plain fade a morph. A dissolve alone moves no geometry; a morph must also warp. The second trap is mismatched control points, which tears the image.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 (digital images), Unit 3 (Bezier curves for shape morphing), Unit 4 (image formats).
chapters.leave: Colour models to Unit 1; compression of the morph frames to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Each look has a technique: 2D uses cels, sprites, cut-outs or rotoscoping, and 3D uses a modelling–rigging–animation–rendering pipeline driven by keyframes, procedures or captured motion.
chapters.depth: 2D techniques: frame-by-frame (cel) animation, sprite animation (small bitmaps moved over a background), cut-out or puppet animation (parts moved on layers), rotoscoping (tracing live footage). 3D pipeline in order: modelling, texturing, rigging, animation, lighting, rendering. Forward kinematics rotates each joint down the chain; inverse kinematics fixes the hand or foot and solves the joint angles backwards. Animation methods: keyframe, procedural (rule or formula driven, e.g. waves), motion capture, and particle systems for fire, smoke and rain. Tool families by job, not by brand. Some syllabi call cut-out animation 'puppet animation' and procedural animation 'expression-driven animation'.

figure.caption: The branch you pick fixes the whole tool chain: 2D works on drawings or sprites, 3D must first build and rig a model.
figure.aria: A tree splitting animation techniques into 2D methods (frame-by-frame, sprite, cut-out, rotoscope) and 3D methods (keyframe with rig, procedural, motion capture).

chapters.example: A 2D cel animation runs 10 s at 24 fps and the animator draws a key pose every 6 frames. Find the number of frames, the number of key poses and the number of in-betweens.
chapters.trap: Mixing up forward and inverse kinematics, and assuming every 3D animation needs motion capture. A rig with keyframes is still 3D animation.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 (rotation, scaling, composite transforms) and Unit 3 (polygon meshes, rendering).
chapters.leave: Shading and hidden surface removal to Unit 3; video codecs to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: An authoring tool's metaphor decides how you organise a title: a stack of cards, a flow of icons, or a timeline of layers.
chapters.depth: Card or page-based tools: the title is a stack of screens joined by buttons and links, one card on screen at a time. Icon or object-based tools: the title is a flowchart of icons, each icon an object with properties, and the authoring warehouse holds the media. Time-based tools: a timeline with layers, a cast of objects and frames, so the title plays by clock time. Cross-platform authoring publishes one project to desktop, web and mobile. Compare the three on structure, ease of change and how interactivity is expressed. Applications to name: interactive presentations, virtual learning modules and simulations, where a simulation reacts to learner input instead of playing a fixed sequence. Some syllabi call page-based tools 'hypermedia authoring' and icon-based tools 'flowchart authoring'.

figure.title: A card-based training title
figure.caption: Each box is one full screen; the dashed arrows are the learner jumping backwards, which a card stack allows and a plain video does not.
figure.aria: A card flow from menu card to lesson card to quiz card to score card, with dashed return links for a wrong answer and for going home.

chapters.example: A training title has 1 menu card, 12 lesson cards, 5 quiz cards and 1 score card. How many cards does the card-based version need, and how long is the same content if rebuilt as a time-based title with 30 s per card?
chapters.trap: Reading 'icon based' as ordinary GUI icons, and 'time based' as 'has a clock'. Also forgetting that a time-based version loses branching.
chapters.prereq: Unit 4 (media types and the elements that go into a title).
chapters.leave: File formats to Unit 4; streaming and delivery to Unit 6; the tools themselves to chapters 5.6 to 5.9.

chapters.idea: Painting and drawing tools differ in what they store — a grid of pixels or a list of objects — and that one choice fixes resolution, editing power and file size.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this chapter, so keep it short. Paint tools change pixels directly: brush, airbrush, eraser, bucket fill, and shapes rendered into the bitmap. Drawing or vector tools keep objects you can re-edit: lines, curves, shapes with fill and stroke. Image editing: selection, crop, resample (changes pixel count, needs interpolation) versus resize (changes print size at fixed pixels), bit depth and colour mode, and simple brightness, contrast and hue shifts. Classify the tool families the syllabi list by the data each stores: painting, drawing, image editing, 3D modelling and animation, audio editing and digital movie tools.

figure.caption: The first branch stores pixels and fixes resolution; the second stores geometry and stays sharp at any size.
figure.aria: A tree of editing tools split into pixel painting, object drawing and whole-image editing, each with its typical tools.

chapters.example: An image is 4 in × 4 in at 300 dpi in 24-bit colour. Find its pixel dimensions and uncompressed size, then the size after resampling to 150 dpi.
chapters.trap: Confusing resample with resize. Lowering dpi without touching pixels keeps the file the same and only changes print size; resampling throws pixels away.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 (raster versus vector graphics, colour models).
chapters.leave: Bezier geometry to chapter 5.8; layer-based retouching to chapter 5.7.

chapters.idea: Retouching stays safe and reversible when each edit lives on its own layer and the colour changes sit in adjustment layers instead of being burned into pixels.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this chapter, so keep it short. Layers form a stack drawn bottom first; each layer has opacity and alpha, and the composite is C = α·C_top + (1 − α)·C_below, per channel, rounded and clamped to 0–255. Layer masks: white shows, black hides, grey blends, so you retouch through the mask and never erase. Blend modes as named formulas: normal, multiply, screen, overlay. Adjustment layers (levels, curves, hue/saturation) affect every layer below and store the correction, not the result; clipping one adjustment to the layer directly beneath is the local fix. Filters are neighbourhood operations: blur, sharpen, noise, unsharp mask. Say why non-destructive editing wins: you can reopen the correction next week.

figure.caption: The correction sits above the photo and the mask limits where the retouch shows, so the original pixels are never overwritten.
figure.aria: A layer stack with a curves adjustment on top affecting all layers, a masked retouch layer in the middle and the original background at the bottom.

chapters.example: A background pixel is (200, 100, 50). A blue fill layer of (0, 0, 255) lies on top at 50% layer opacity, and the mask is 40% white at that spot. Find the composite pixel.
chapters.trap: Forgetting that an unclipped adjustment layer changes everything below it, and ignoring the clamp to 0–255 when adding layers, which is where clipped highlights come from.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 5.6 for pixel tools, Unit 1 for the RGB colour model.
chapters.leave: Colour model conversions to Unit 1; file formats and compression to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: A vector path is a list of anchor points joined by Bezier segments, and the pen tool is just a way of placing an anchor and dragging its handles to set the tangent.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this chapter, so keep it short. Anatomy of a path: anchor points, handles (control points), segments. A smooth point has its two handles in a straight line, a corner point does not. Open versus closed paths, fill versus stroke, path operations (union, subtract, intersect) and converting a path into a selection. Give the cubic Bezier formula B(t) = (1 − t)³P₀ + 3t(1 − t)²P₁ + 3t²(1 − t)P₂ + t³P₃ for 0 ≤ t ≤ 1, with each term named, and evaluate it by de Casteljau or by direct substitution. The tangent at t = 0 points along P₁ − P₀. Explain why vector art scales: the geometry is stored, so it is re-rendered at any size. Some syllabi call anchors 'nodes' and handles 'direction lines'.

figure.title: Using the pen tool
figure.caption: The drag in step two is what bends the segment; a click with no drag gives a straight corner.
figure.aria: A five-step pen tool flow: click an anchor, drag a handle, add segments, close the path, then fill or stroke it.

chapters.example: A cubic Bezier has P₀(0, 0), P₁(0, 50), P₂(50, 50), P₃(50, 0). Find the point at t = 0.5 and the tangent direction at t = 0.
chapters.trap: Assuming a handle pulls the curve through itself. The curve does not pass through P₁ or P₂; they only set the pull. Also calling a path a selection — they are different objects.
chapters.prereq: Unit 3 (Bezier curves and surfaces), Unit 1 (raster versus vector).
chapters.leave: Bezier surfaces and B-splines to Unit 3; pixel painting to chapter 5.6.

chapters.idea: On a timeline, a motion tween interpolates a symbol's properties between two keyframes along a path, and motion blur fakes speed by smearing the object over the shutter time.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this chapter, so keep it short. Timeline parts: frames, keyframes, layers, frame rate, playhead. Motion tween on a symbol instance (position, scale, rotation, alpha, filters, colour) versus shape tween on raw shapes. The tween path and its easing curve, swapping the tween target without redrawing, and nested animations where a symbol carries its own inner timeline. Animating transformations and filters, and 3D motion along the z axis. Motion blur: shutter angle and shutter time, blur length ≈ speed × shutter time. Testing the movie at the target frame rate. Buttons, stop actions, ActionScript and publishing are named only; they are outside this unit's scope.

figure.caption: Two keyframes hold the ends of the ball tween; every frame between them is computed, and the text layer runs on its own shorter span.
figure.aria: A timeline with a ball layer holding keyframes at frames 1 and 24 with a motion tween between them, and a text layer with a shape tween over frames 1 to 12.

chapters.example: A symbol tweens from x = 100 px to x = 400 px over 24 frames at 24 fps. Find its average speed, then the motion blur length with a 1/48 s shutter.
chapters.trap: Putting a motion tween on a raw shape (it needs a symbol instance), and quoting the tween length in frames when the question asks for seconds.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 5.2 (keyframes and interpolation), chapter 5.4 (2D/3D techniques), Unit 4 (video formats and frame rates).
chapters.leave: Button code, ActionScript, sound and video import, and publishing are outside this unit; streaming and delivery belong to Unit 6.
